content.page_title: Diagnosis and treatment of pulmonary embolism (PE) in pregnancy (excerpt)

ventilation_lung_scan.notes: Values from table at top of page (approximate)

CTPA.notes: Computed tomography pulmonary angiography; values approximate from table

diagnostic_imaging_findings_and_recommen: A normal perfusion scan and a negative CTPA appear equally safe for ruling out PE in pregnancy based on retrospective series.
Inconclusive imaging results are a known problem (reported rates up to about one-third of investigations, especially late in pregnancy).
V/Q SPECT is associated with low foetal and maternal radiation exposure and shows promise for PE diagnosis in pregnancy, but further evaluation is needed before widespread adoption.

MRA: long-term effects of gadolinium contrast on the foetus are unknown; technically inadequate images and high rates of inconclusive results have been reported in non-pregnant patients, so MRA cannot currently be recommended for diagnosing or ruling out PE in pregnancy.
Conventional pulmonary angiography involves significantly higher foetal radiation exposure (reported ≈2.2–3.7 mSv in the text) and should be avoided during pregnancy.
clinical_considerations_and_risks: Overdiagnosis of PE in pregnancy can have significant, lifelong implications (e.g., bleeding risk at delivery, withholding oestrogen contraception, requirement for future thromboprophylaxis).
Choice of initial imaging should consider local expertise and resources due to variable rates of inadequate/indeterminate CTPA and scintigraphy scans.
treatment_recommendations_for_PE_in_preg: Low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) is the treatment of choice for PE during pregnancy.
LMWH does not cross the placenta and therefore does not confer a risk of foetal haemorrhage or teratogenicity.
Unfractionated heparin (UFH) is also considered safe in pregnancy, but LMWH has more predictable pharmacokinetics and a more favourable risk profile.

No randomized controlled trial has established the optimal LMWH dose for PE in pregnancy; published data favour dosing similar to non-pregnant patients, with once-daily (o.d.) or twice-daily (b.i.d.) regimens based on early pregnancy weight.
For the majority of patients receiving LMWH for PE in pregnancy, current practice follows dosing approaches used in non-pregnant patients (references cited in guideline).
